title: Protecting the Plan/Act Boundary in a Bug-Fix Coding Agent Workflow
description: Tests the ability to design a coding-agent workflow that separates reasoning (which can be wrong) from action (which is irreversible), scope each agent's tools to its role, place review checkpoints correctly, and preserve a reconstructable audit trail.

scenario.background: Priya, a platform lead at a mid-size logistics company, is standing up her team's first coding-agent workflow for bug-fix tasks. She configures a planner custom agent with read-only tools (grep, glob, view) and an executor custom agent with edit and bash access in addition. An engineer files an issue asking to fix a failing shipment-status test by adding a missing enum value, explicitly scoping the change to one file and its test, and explicitly prohibiting any change to the public API surface.

characters.name: Priya Malhotra
characters.concern: Wants fast, low-friction bug fixes without giving up an auditable, reconstructable trail of what the agent actually did and why.

characters.name: Alex Kim
characters.concern: Needs to be able to check a proposed plan or diff quickly, without needing to have watched the session live.

questions.stem: Why does the planner agent only having read-only tools (grep, glob, view) matter for this workflow's safety?
options: It doesn't matter — the planner's tool access is irrelevant since it never takes real actions anyway

It structurally guarantees the planning phase cannot make any edit, regardless of what the agent reasons its way into wanting to do — the boundary between reasoning and action is enforced by tool capability, not by hoping the agent behaves
It's only there to make the planner run faster, since fewer tools means less overhead
It exists purely to reduce token costs during planning, with no safety implication
questions.explanation: B is correct because a planner restricted to read-only tools physically cannot edit anything no matter what its plan concludes — this is the core mechanism that separates agent reasoning (which can be wrong or overconfident) from agent action (which is irreversible), enforced structurally rather than through instruction alone. A dismisses a real safety design choice as irrelevant. C and D both miss that the tool restriction is a deliberate safety boundary, not a performance or cost optimization.

questions.stem: Alex reviews the planner's proposed plan in under a minute before it's approved. What makes this review fast and effective?
options: Alex has to re-read the entire codebase from scratch to verify the plan

The plan is checked against the issue's explicit constraints (right files touched, no destructive operations, no public API change) — a well-scoped input and an implicit success criterion make the check fast because there's a small, specific thing to verify
Alex trusts the plan automatically since the planner agent is read-only
The review is fast because Alex skips checking whether the plan matches the issue's stated constraints
questions.explanation: B is correct because the issue gave the workflow a well-scoped input and an implicit success criterion (the named test passes, no public API change), which means the plan review has a small, specific, checkable target — right files, no destructive operations, no API-surface change — rather than an open-ended judgment call. A describes an unnecessarily slow, unscoped review. C substitutes blind trust in the tool restriction for actually checking the plan's content, which isn't what the scenario describes happening. D describes skipping the review's actual purpose entirely.

questions.stem: After the executor implements the change and opens a draft PR, a teammate reviews it asynchronously and marks it ready. Why does the PR still need a human approval before merging, even though the plan was already approved?
options: Because the branch-protection ruleset only lists the agent's own working-branch pushes in the bypass list, not the required-review rule for merges into main — plan approval and merge approval are two separate checkpoints
It doesn't need another approval — plan approval should be sufficient to also authorize the merge
Because the executor agent is inherently untrustworthy regardless of any configuration
Because GitHub requires two approvals for every PR by default, unrelated to this workflow's design
questions.explanation: A is correct because the workflow deliberately keeps plan approval and merge approval as two separate checkpoints — the branch-protection ruleset's bypass list only covers the agent's own branch pushes, not the required review for merging into main, so a human still has to approve before the change reaches the protected branch. B collapses two intentionally separate checkpoints into one, weakening the safeguard. C mischaracterizes a deliberate two-checkpoint design as blanket distrust. D invents a generic GitHub default rather than describing this workflow's actual, deliberately configured ruleset.

questions.stem: What makes the entire sequence — plan, execution, PR, review, merge — reconstructable months later without anyone needing to remember what happened?
options: The plan artifact, commits, diff, PR comments, and session log are all durable records living in Git and GitHub, not in anyone's memory or the session's own transient state
Nothing is reconstructable after the session ends — this workflow relies on institutional memory
Only the final merged diff matters; the plan and intermediate comments are discarded once the PR merges
A separate audit database outside GitHub tracks the full history
questions.explanation: A is correct because every artifact that mattered — the plan, the commits, the PR thread, the session log — is durable state stored directly in Git and GitHub rather than living only in a session's transient memory or a person's recollection, which is exactly what makes the sequence reconstructable long after the fact. B contradicts what the scenario describes. C discards the plan and review context that explain *why* the diff looks the way it does, which is needed for a full reconstruction. D invents infrastructure not described in the scenario — the actual audit trail lives in GitHub itself.

keyLearnings: Separating a read-only planning phase from an edit-capable execution phase enforces the reasoning/action boundary structurally, via tool capability, not via instructions the agent might not follow.
A well-scoped issue with explicit constraints turns plan review into a small, fast, specific check instead of an open-ended judgment call.

Plan approval and merge approval are two separate checkpoints for a reason — branch-protection rules should not let an agent's own working-branch bypass extend to bypassing required review on the protected branch.
A reconstructable audit trail comes from every artifact (plan, commits, diff, comments, session log) living as durable state in Git and GitHub, not in anyone's memory.
